claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 has an initially homogeneous, metastable, high-temperature single-phase BCC state.
Cooling or moderate thermal exposure causes spinodal decomposition of the metastable BCC state in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7.
Atomic size mismatch involving Cr and Al produces local lattice distortions and chemical heterogeneities.
The cited size-mismatch evidence specifically identifies Cr as a major source of lattice distortion in this alloy.
Local lattice distortions and chemical heterogeneities lower the energy barrier for nucleation of secondary phases.
The secondary phases may include ordered B2 or other intermetallic-like domains within the BCC matrix.
A rapid quench will retain a uniform single-phase BCC baseline with homogeneous lattice parameters and defect density.
Slow cooling or annealing between 740 K and 1000 K permits diffusion and local compositional fluctuations that promote decomposition.
Relatively short thermal treatments reaching 1000 K can leave an alloy far from equilibrium.
The mechanism will be suppressed by sufficiently rapid quenching because atomic mobility is limited.
The mechanism will not operate outside the temperature range in which differential diffusivities are significant.
The interplay between lattice misfit and differential atomic mobility produces spinodal-like decomposition in the BCC structure.
Local strain fields facilitate nucleation and growth of secondary phases in confined domains.
BCC material can decompose into distinct BCC structures during short heat treatments.
Slow-cooled or moderately annealed specimens will show new diffraction peaks or lattice-parameter shifts relative to the quenched baseline.
Slow-cooled or moderately annealed specimens will show microscopy-visible compositional or structural inhomogeneities.
Slow-cooled or moderately annealed specimens will exhibit altered hardness correlated with phase changes.
Increasing Al content in Al-Co-Cr-Fe-Ni alloys can enhance BCC formation and increase hardness.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis labels the transformation as spinodal decomposition while repeatedly describing reduced nucleation barriers and nucleation-and-growth. Classical spinodal decomposition is barrierless and does not proceed by nucleation, so the proposed mechanism conflates two distinct transformation modes.
